title: the Lalita Sahasranama (selections)
hook: a war told in names, and the surprising last act after the battle: love brought back from ash

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama and the four hands: the noose that is desire, the goad that is anger, the bow that is the mind. Did a want turn up that you could see as held? Day one thousand one hundred three.

What happens to love after it's been burned to ash? In the old stories, Kama, the god of love, once aimed his flower arrows at Shiva while Shiva sat in meditation. Shiva opened his third eye, and Kama was burned to nothing. The story told alongside the Lalita Sahasranama picks up from there. Tradition says something grew out of those ashes: a demon named Bhanda, who brought misery to the worlds until the gods offered themselves into a sacrificial fire and the goddess Lalita rose from it. Then comes a war. And the hymn, which is mostly names, tells that war in names too. Today, the battle, and what she does after it.
screen: `KAMA BURNED TO ASH.` → `A DEMON FROM THE ASHES.` → `A WAR TOLD IN NAMES.`

segments.voice: Read a stretch of the hymn slowly and the story moves under the names like a river under ice. In paraphrase: she delights in the courage of her powers as they cut down Bhanda's army. She delights in the young goddess Bala, who strikes down Bhanda's sons. She glances at the face of Kameshvara, her consort, and from that glance Ganesha is formed. She rejoices when Ganesha shatters the device the demons built to block her army. And then the end of the war: with Kameshvara's own weapon she burns Bhanda, and his city with him. The gods praise her glory. That would be a fine place to finish. A demon is gone. The worlds are safe. But the hymn adds one more name, and it's the surprise. In paraphrase: she is the life-giving herb for Kama, who was burned by the fire of Shiva's eye. After the battle, she brings love back. Hold that next to yesterday. Lalita carries a sugarcane bow and flower arrows, the same things Kama carried. The hymn doesn't treat desire as the enemy to be destroyed forever. What grew wrong out of the ash is defeated, and the one who was burned is restored. Readers take the turn in more than one way. Some read it inwardly: the ego's monster is ended, and love, made whole, can live again. Others keep it as story: the goddess is the power who can raise what was turned to ash. And some readers simply notice the order. The hymn won't let a war be the last word about her. Healing is.
screen: `HER POWERS CUT DOWN BHANDA'S ARMY.` · `GANESHA BREAKS THE BLOCKING DEVICE.` · `BHANDA AND HIS CITY BURN.` · `THEN SHE BRINGS KAMA BACK.` · then, large: `THE LIFE-GIVING HERB FOR KAMA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: after the battle. Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind something in your own life that once burned out: a friendship gone quiet, an old enthusiasm, a hope you set down. Don't argue with it. Just let it be there, the way ash is there after a fire. Then, without forcing anything, ask what small part of it might still be alive. A memory. A name. One phone number. Rest with that. If you pray, you can bring it before the goddess, or before God, in your own words. If you don't, let the question stay open. The bell holds the time.
The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn of names that tells a war, and ends the war with Kama, love, brought back from ash. Today's word.
Your line: the Lalita Sahasranama, in selections. Today, after something hard is over, look for one thing to restore, not just one thing to finish. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: The story of Lalita's war with Bhanda is told in the Lalitopakhyana of the Brahmanda Purana, and devotees who recite the Lalita Sahasranama pass through the battle in a run of its names.

original.note: Sanskrit kāma: desire, love; also the name of the god of love, who carries a sugarcane bow and flower arrows.

trapdoor: what you thought: a goddess story that ends when the demon dies.
what it means: after the battle, the hymn names her as the one who brings Kama, love, back from the ash.
what a scholar hears: kāmeśvarāstranirdagdhasabhaṇḍāsuraśūnyakā, then haranetrāgnisaṃdagdhakāmasañjīvanauṣadhiḥ: the war's end and the revival, a few names apart.

notes: Names paraphrased: bhaṇḍasainyavadhodyuktaśaktivikramaharṣitā; bhaṇḍaputravadhodyuktabālāvikramananditā; kāmeśvaramukhālokakalpitaśrīgaṇeśvarā; mahāgaṇeśanirbhinnavighnayantrapraharṣitā; kāmeśvarāstranirdagdhasabhaṇḍāsuraśūnyakā; brahmopendramahendrādidevasaṃstutavaibhavā; haranetrāgnisaṃdagdhakāmasañjīvanauṣadhiḥ. Confirm order and the approximate range given in sources.

Story frame (Kama burned by Shiva's third eye; Bhanda arising from his ashes; the gods' sacrifice; Lalita rising from the fire) is from the Lalitopakhyana; Bhanda's origin is attributed as 'tradition says'. Confirm details, including the role of the gana Chitrakarma, deliberately left out.
Śūnyaka is Bhanda's city; 'burns Bhanda, and his city with him' paraphrases the name. Confirm.
Three readings (inward; story of restoring power; the order of the names) attributed to commentators and 'some readers' without naming one. Confirm fair.
The line 'the hymn won't let a war be the last word about her' refers only to this sequence; the hymn continues for many names after.

Editor pass: 'Commentators read' changed to 'Readers take' (no commentary named); source range widened to c. 64–84 so it includes the Kama-revival name (haranetrāgni…, c. 84). The hymn also has names between Ganesha and the burning of Bhanda (e.g. the ten avatars from her fingernails), skipped here; 'And then the end of the war' covers the gap.
